extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and performers wanting practical guidance on writing and performing humor
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, workbook-style guidance for creating, refining, performing, and selling comedy material across stand-up, scripts, speeches, and one-person shows. Emphasizes joke structure, daily exercises, performance technique, and career-building steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find your authentic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Find your “authentic” voice—the true source of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sincere instead of merely trying to be funny; speak from what is real for you and avoid pandering or mismatch between persona and material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate comedy genre/medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which genre of comedy writing or performing suits you best and tailor material for each: stand-up, script, speech and joke writing, one-person shows, humor essays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book presents pros and cons of various comedy fields and directs you how to develop, refine, and sell work specific to each medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke structure: setup, turn, tag
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke has a setup, turn and a tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this basic three-part structure to construct jokes; ensure each part serves its role (setup establishes, turn surprises, tag extends the laugh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-part joke breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are broken down into five parts: Attitude, topic, premise, act-out, mix, act-out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the listed elements to analyze and build jokes; note the book's framing of attitude/topic/premise as the serious setup and act-out/mix as the funny bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic and attitude selection
rubrics_metrics.description: What the joke is about is called the topic. It has one of four basic attitudes: weird, scary, hard, stupid. (“You know what’s weird/scary/hard/stupid about ______?”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a clear attitude+topic combination to frame your premise; using these attitude categories helps create a recognizable setup for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise qualities (opinion/original observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A premise is also called an opinion, a point of view. It must clearly and precisely answer the question of the attitude+topic. It’s usually more insightful than funny. A good premise is also an original observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premises should be cut-to-the-chase and original; they should not be mere descriptions or long stories—they set the intellectual hook that the funniness builds on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first-person in the premise
rubrics_metrics.description: I, me or my in the premise, it’s too self-absorbed and won’t interest the audience. Once the audience is interested, you can bring in specific personal elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the premise general enough to engage the audience; introduce personal specifics only after establishing relatable ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: General-to-specific progression
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke starts out general so everyone can relate, and after the premise is the time to bring in the specifics about you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open broad to pull in the audience, then narrow toward personal detail for surprise and uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act-out vs. explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure you are in fact doing an act-out and not explaining. Become the type of person you are joking about rather than describing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform the scene or behavior (act-out) instead of narrating it; this creates immediacy and laughs rather than distant description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixes and 'what if' constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixes generally start with “What if,” and are most always followed by another act-out. Another way to do a mix is to change the environment (e.g., put your self-absorbed mother in a different occupation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mixes to juxtapose contexts or compare two things for comedic surprise; follow with vivid act-outs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All topics need to be relatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatability helps audiences connect; beware that highly universal topics risk feeling 'hack'—balance universality with original perspective to avoid clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mine life/pain for material
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost everything (and anything) in your life can be turned into a comedy topic if you care about it enough. The more painful or humiliating something is, the more likely it is to make an audience laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal, vulnerable material as a rich source of comedy but shape it into a premise and act-out so it serves the joke rather than self-indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze other comics systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch your favorite comic and write a few of their jokes and answers to these questions: Is their attitude stated or implied? Is there an act-out? A mix? Where do they get the most laughs? What personal details did you learn? What did they do to get the laughs? What topics did they use? What are their signature topics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deconstruct effective performers to learn patterns, pacing, and choices you can adapt—not copy—from their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sincere rather than prioritizing 'being funny'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sincere instead of funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity builds rapport; an honest perspective often yields stronger comedic material than forced joke-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecation for rapport
rubrics_metrics.description: The best person to poke fun at is you. That’s how you get the audience’s sympathy, rapport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-targeting to build goodwill, but avoid undermining material that prevents the audience from rooting for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targets must 'deserve it'
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s no such thing as a victimless joke. Each joke has a target and you have to make sure that whoever or whatever that target is—they deserve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ethical and practical effects of targets; avoid punching down in ways that alienate your audience or make them uncomfortable to laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid props; use mime/description
rubrics_metrics.description: Props aren’t worth the schlep and can ruin your timing when you go looking for them. They also create a disconnection from the audience. Rather than showing the audience the big stupid hat your mother wore, describe and mime it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on imagination and physicality instead of lugging props; often description plus mime yields a bigger laugh than a literal prop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorization via chunking
rubrics_metrics.description: How do I memorize my act? Break it into chunks that make sense, such as four categories—special challenges, childhood, current issue, and relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group material into thematic blocks to aid recall and to structure a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance attitude, timing, and audience interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing... Don’t talk while the audience is laughing. Stand-up is not a monologue—it’s a dialogue with the audience. You talk, then the audience talks (by laughing), and then you respond to the audience. There should never be even one moment when you’re onstage and attitude free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat laughter as part of the rhythm; maintain a clear attitude onstage and use tags while laughter occurs instead of talking over it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make rehearsed material sound spontaneous; use present tense
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if your jokes are rehearsed, they have to sound spontaneous to sound real. Make sure all your jokes are in the present tense: 'I am' rather than 'I was.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice to the point of naturalness; present-tense phrasing keeps material feeling immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with room observation and sustainable tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with something that is obvious about the room. Make sure your opening sets a tone that you can sustain. And don’t assume the audience is interested in you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topical or situational openings to get on the audience's wavelength, but be ready to abandon opening bits if they clash with the room's mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid filler between jokes; use attitude segues
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need for anything in between jokes. If a sentence is not part of a joke, then it’s part of a problem. If you feel the need to use words in between jokes, then use an attitude word to segue: 'And you know what else is stupid … ?' or 'Another weird thing is …'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep momentum by making every line earn its place; use attitude bridges rather than neutral chatter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite, cut, and prune relentlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating great material is all about rewriting, cutting and pruning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively edit to tighten setups, remove excess words, and sharpen punchlines; perform and then cut based on audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comedic devices: callbacks, lists of three, runners
rubrics_metrics.description: A callback is when you call back, or mention again, something you brought up earlier. List of three: set up a pattern on the first two ideas and then turn it on the third. A runner is a catchphrase that runs through your stint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ these proven devices for structure and amplified payoff (example: 'Bears, beats, Battlestar Galactica').

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily exercises and brainstorming routines
rubrics_metrics.description: In the morning, spend ten minutes writing stream of consciousness. Write ten 'what if’s.' Pick at least two current-events topics and write ten opinions about each. Record yourself ranting for ten minutes about one topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, frequent exercises to generate ideas, loosen creativity, and produce raw material to refine later.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-person show criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the difference with a one-person show? Don’t have to make the audience laugh the whole time; Tell a dramatic story, using humor; Audience doesn’t have to be included. A person doing a solo show takes the audience on a journey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing a solo piece, prioritize narrative arc and emotional stakes as much as laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech-specific: end with a 'heart story'
rubrics_metrics.description: In a speech, end your talk with a 'heart story.' This is something that will move them emotionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an emotionally resonant anecdote to close speeches for impact and memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal-setting and measurable practice plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Goal sheet: this week I will - write for ________ minutes each morning - create ________ pages/minutes of new material - perform ________ times - try out ________ new jokes - call at least ________ new people to help my career. My ultimate career goals are ___. In order to achieve these, the actions I need to take are ___.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set concrete, measurable weekly goals (writing minutes, creations, performances, networking) and list actions to achieve career aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentorship and feedback protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Get a mentor. Seek them out. Buy them lunch. Tell them specifically what you like about their… Do not ask them to do something for you. Only if you get a return email. Also, just ask for honest feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach mentors humbly, ask for specific critique, offer something in return, and request actionable feedback rather than favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting current-event material by opinion not inherent funniness
rubrics_metrics.description: How to pick a current-event topic: (1) don’t pick one because you think is funny. There is no such thing as a funny topic. There are no funny ideas. It’s what you do with an idea that makes it funny. (2) Don’t pick weird topics, but rather have unique opinions about ordinary topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn news stories into premises by extracting a clear opinion or reaction; use exercises (e.g., read USA Today and turn points into premises) to generate material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy writing toolbox (supplies & idea-book)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy supplies: pen, pocket notebook, large binder, 100 index cards, voice recorder/phone. Keeping an Idea Book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always capture ideas physically or digitally; organize fragments on index cards or in a binder for later editing and performance testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards: reject gross-out/blue/hack material
rubrics_metrics.description: Carter draws the line at gross-out humor, nay-says blue routines, and calls out hack jokes for what they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain higher comedic standards; avoid lazy, mean-spirited, or gratuitously offensive material that alienates audiences or degrades craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching, selling, and career/business skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a finished product to the next level—making money—by pitching it to a buyer and negotiating a contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how to package work for buyers, understand market expectations, and negotiate terms; the book includes practical tips from industry pros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec-script strategy (debated guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book contains a long section on crafting a spec script based for an existing TV show (though reviewers note industry advice often favors writing an original spec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this advice may be dated or contested; consider current industry norms (many recommend original specs) before following older templates.
